notes.meaning: The wall is finished and the doors now hang in the gates. Nehemiah then sets the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites (helpers at the temple from the tribe of Levi) in their places. Some think they were given the unusual job of guarding the city walls and gates. Others think they went back to their temple work or got ready for the wall's dedication. Either way, God's worship was the city's real defense and its reason for being.

Nehemiah was probably about to go back to the Persian court, so he left two trusted men in charge. Hanani was his brother, the man who first brought him news of Jerusalem's ruin. Hananiah commanded the fortress near the temple. He was chosen because he was faithful and feared God more than most. Nehemiah trusted that this deep respect for God would keep him loyal once Nehemiah was gone.

City gates in that part of the world usually opened at sunrise. Nehemiah told them to wait until it was full daylight, when people were up and any enemy could be seen coming. The doors were to be shut and barred while the guards stood by. Ordinary residents would take turns on watch, each near his own home, where he would care most. Matthew Henry adds a lesson: a community stays safe when each person guards himself and his family against sin.

The new wall followed the old lines, so it closed in a wide area. But few people lived inside it. Saying the houses were not rebuilt does not mean there were none at all. It means there were not nearly enough, and many were rough huts with empty ground between them. Nehemiah built the walls in faith, trusting God's promise to fill the city again.

Nehemiah gives God the credit even for a common-sense plan. Every good idea in our minds comes from God. He gathered the leaders and the people to list them by family line. This would help him find families who could move into Jerusalem, and it would show who was allowed to serve as priests. A city's safety depends more on its people than on its walls. While doing this, he found the old record of the first group who came back from exile, the same list found in Ezra 2.

Here begins the copied list. These were people of Judah who came home from Babylon in the first group, led by Zerubbabel and Jeshua, about ninety years earlier. A few leaders' names are spelled differently in Ezra 2:2, such as Azariah for Seraiah. The Nehemiah named here is likely an earlier leader, not the cupbearer who wrote this book. Only a small share of the exiles came back. These pioneers left comfort behind to answer God's call.

The count of families begins, each named after a forefather. This list is almost exactly the same as Ezra 2. Repeating it shows how God delights in his people and notices each family. It also reminded them of their small beginnings, so they could thank God for how he had grown them.

The family counts continue. A few numbers here differ a little from Ezra 2. Some explain this by mistakes in copying, since numbers are easy to miscopy. Others think one list was made in Babylon and the other later in Judea. Most of the figures match exactly.

More families are named and counted. A long list like this shows that each person matters to God. He knows his people by name, as Jesus said of his sheep. Families matter to him too. Nothing about God's people is too small for him to record.

The list goes on with some of the largest families. For Bigvai, some old copies read 2,066, the same as Ezra 2:14. Keeping these family records was important, because they had to be kept until the Messiah came.

More families are listed, some of them quite small. Matthew Henry gives thanks that our faith does not rest on getting every name and number exactly right. It rests on the great truths of God's law and the gospel. Still, God never forgets those who serve him.

This part of the list ends with two more families. Hariph is likely the same family called Jorah in Ezra 2:18. In Jewish custom one person could go by different names. That helps explain some of the small differences between the two lists.
